div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: A drawing-room in Sir John Vesey's house; folding-doors at the back, which open on another drawing-room. To the right a table, with newspapers, books, &c.; to the left a sofa writing-table.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN
sp.p: Yes, he says at two precisely. “Dear Sir John, as since the death of my sainted Maria,”—Hum—that's his wife; she made him a martyr, and now he makes her a saint!

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: Well, as since her death?—

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN
sp.p: “I have been living in chambers, where I cannot so well invite ladies, you will allow me to bring Mr. Sharp, the lawyer, to read the will of the late Mr. Mordaunt (to which I am appointed executor) at your house—your daughter being the nearest relation. I shall be with you at two precisely. Henry Graves.”

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: And you really feel sure that poor Mr. Mordaunt has made me his heiress?

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Ay, the richest heiress in England. Can you doubt it? Are you not his nearest relation? Niece by your poor mother, his own sister. All the time he was making this enormous fortune in India did we ever miss sending him little reminiscences of our disinterested affection? When he was last in England, and you only so high, was not my house his home? Didn't I get a surfeit out of complaisance to his execrable curries and pillaws? Didn't he smoke his hookah—nasty old —that is, poor dear man—in my best drawing-room? And did you ever speak without calling him your “handsome uncle?”—for the excellent creature was as vain as a peacock,—

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: And so ugly,—

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: The dear deceased! Alas, he was, indeed, like a kangaroo in a jaundice! And if, after all these marks of attachment, you are not his heiress, why then the finest feelings of our nature—the ties of blood—the principles of justice—are implanted in us in vain.

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: Beautiful, sir. Was not that in your last speech at the Freemasons' Tavern upon the great Chimney-sweep Question?

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Clever girl!—what a memory she has! Sit down, Georgy. Upon this most happy—I mean melancholy —occasion, I feel that I may trust you with a secret. You see this fine house—our fine servants—our fine plate—our fine dinners: every one thinks Sir John Vesey a rich man.

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: And are you not, papa?

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Not a bit of it—all humbug, child,—all humbug, upon my soul! As you hazard a minnow to hook in a trout, so one guinea thrown out with address is often the best bait for a hundred. There are two rules in life—First, Men are valued not for what they are, but what they seem to be. Secondly, If you have no merit or money of your own, you must trade on the merits and money of other people. My father got the title by services in the army, and died penniless. On the strength of his services I got a pension of 400l. a-year—on the strength of 400l. a-year I took credit for 800l.: on the strength of 800l. a-year I married your mother with 10,000l.: on the strength of 10,000l. I took credit for 40,000l., and paid Dicky Gossip three guineas a-week to go about everywhere calling me “Stingy Jack.”

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: Ha! ha! A disagreeable nickname.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN
sp.p: But a valuable reputation. When a man is called stingy, it is as much as calling him rich; and when a man's called rich, why he's a man universally respected. On the strength of my respectability I wheedled a constituency, changed my politics, resigned my seat to a minister, who, to a man of such stake in the country, could offer nothing less in return than a patent office of 2000l. a-year. That's the way to succeed in life. Humbug, my dear!—all humbug, upon my soul!

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: I must say that you—

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN,
sp.p: Know the world, to be sure. Now, for your fortune, as I spend all that I have, I can have nothing to leave you; yet even without counting your uncle, you have always passed for an heiress on the credit of your expectations from the savings of “Stingy Jack.” The same with your education. I never grudged anything to make a show—never stuffed your head with histories and homilies; but you draw, you sing, you dance, you walk well into a room; and that's the way young ladies are educated now-a-days, in order to become a pride to their parents and a blessing to their husband—that is, when they have caught him. Apropos of a husband: you know we thought of Sir Frederick Blount.

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: Ah, papa, he is charming.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: He was so, my dear, before we knew your poor uncle was dead; but an heiress such as you will be should look out for a duke.—Where the deuce is Evelyn this morning?

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: I've not seen him, papa. What a strange character he is—so sarcastic; and yet he can be agreeable.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: A humorist—a cynic! one never knows how to take him. My private secretary,—a poor cousin,—has not got a shilling, and yet, hang me if he does not keep us all at a sort of a distance.

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: But why do you take him to live with us, papa, since there's no good to be got by it?

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: There you are wrong; he has a great deal of talent: prepares my speeches, writes my pamphlets, looks up my calculations. My report on the last Commission has got me a great deal of fame, and has put me at the head of the new one. Besides, he is our cousin—he has no salary: kindness to a poor relation always tells well in the world; and benevolence is an useful virtue, particularly when you can have it for nothing. With our other cousin, Clara, it was different: her father thought fit to leave me her guardian, though she had not a penny—a mere useless incumbrance; so, you see, I got my half-sister, Lady Franklin, to take her off my my hands.

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: How much longer is Lady Franklin's visit to be?

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: I don't know, my dear; the longer the better, for her husband left her a good deal of money at her own disposal. Ah, here she comes.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Lady Franklin, Clara, Sir John, Georgina.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: My dear sister, we were just loud in your praises. But how's this?—not in mourning?

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Why should I go into mourning for a man I never saw?

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Still there may be a legacy.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Then there'll be less cause for affliction. Ha! ha! my dear Sir John, I'm one of those who think feelings a kind of property, and never take credit for them upon false pretences.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN
sp.p: Very silly woman! But, Clara, I see you are more attentive to the proper decorum; yet you are very, very, VERY distantly connected with the deceased—a third cousin, I think.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Mr. Mordaunt once assisted my father, and these poor robes are all the gratitude I can show him.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Gratitude! humph! I am afraid the minx has got expectations.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: So, Mr. Graves is the executor—the will is addressed to him? The same Mr. Graves who is always in black —always lamenting his ill fortune and his sainted Maria, who led him the life of a dog?

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: The very same. His liveries are black—his carriage is black—he always rides a black galloway—and, faith, if he ever marry again, I think he will show his respect to the sainted Maria by marrying a black woman.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Ha! ha! we shall see.—
Poor Graves, I always liked him: he made an excellent husband.

div.stage: Enter Evelyn (seats himself, and takes up a book, unobserved).

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: What a crowd of relations this Will brings to light: Mr. Stout, the Political Economist—Lord Glossmore—

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Whose grandfather kept a pawnbroker's shop, and who, accordingly, entertains the profoundest contempt for everything popular, parvenu, and plebeian.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Sir Frederick Blount—

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Sir Fwedewick Blount, who objects to the letter R as being too wough, and therefore dwops its acquaintance: one of the new class of prudent young gentlemen, who, not having spirits and constitution for the hearty excesses of their predecessors, entrench themselves in the dignity of a lady-like languor. A man of fashion in the last century was riotous and thoughtless—in this he is tranquil and egotistical. He never does anything that is silly, or says anything that is wise. I beg your pardon, my dear; I believe Sir Frederick is an admirer of yours, provided, on reflection, he does not see “what harm it could do him” to fall in love with your beauty and expectations. Then, too, our poor cousin the scholar,— Oh, Mr. Evelyn, there you are!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Evelyn—the very person I wanted: where have you been all day? Have you seen to those papers?—have you written my epitaph on poor Mordaunt?—Latin you know!—have you reported my speech at Exeter Hall?—have you looked out the debates on the Customs? —and, oh, have you mended up all the old pens in the study?

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: And have you brought me the black floss silk?— have you been to Storr's for my ring?—and, as we cannot go out on this melancholy occasion, did you call at Hookham's for the last H. B. and the Comic Annual?

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: And did you see what was really the matter with my bay horse?—did you get me the Opera-box?—did you buy my little Charley his peg-top?

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: Certainly, Paley is right upon that point; for, put the syllogism thus—
Ma'am—Sir— Miss Vesey—you want something of me?—Paley observes, that to assist even the undeserving tends to the better regulation of our charitable feelings—no apologies—I am quite at your service.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Now he's in one of his humours!

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: You allow him strange liberties, Sir John.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: You will be the less surprised at that, madam, when I inform you that Sir John allows me nothing else.— I am now about to draw on his benevolence.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: I beg your pardon, sir, and like your spirit. Sir John, I'm in the way, I see; for I know your benevolence is so delicate that you never allow any one to detect it!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: I could not do your commissions to-day—I have been to visit a poor woman, who was my nurse and my mother's last friend. She is very poor, very—sick —dying—and she owes six months' rent!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: You know I should be most happy to do anything for yourself. But the nurse—
(some people's nurses are always ill!)—there are so many impostors about!—We'll talk of it to-morrow. This most mournful occasion takes up all my attention.
Bless me! so late! I've letters to write, and—none of the pens are mended?

sp.speaker: GEORGINA
sp.p: I think I will give it to him—And yet, if I don't get the fortune after all!—Papa allows me so little!— then I must have those earrings
. Mr. Evelyn, what is the address of your nurse?

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: She has a good heart with all her foibles!—Ah! Miss Vesey, if that poor woman had not closed the eyes of my lost mother, Alfred Evelyn would not have been this beggar to your father.

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: I will certainly attend to it—
if I get the fortune.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN
sp.p: Georgy, I say.

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: Yes, papa.

div.stage: Evelyn has seated himself again at the table (to the right), and leans his face on his hands.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: His noble spirit bowed to this!—Ah, at least here I may give him comfort—
But he will recognise my hand.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: What bill are you paying, Clara?—putting up a bank-note?

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Hush!—O Lady Franklin, you are the kindest of human beings. This is for a poor person—I would not have her know whence it came, or she would refuse it Would you?—No,—he knows her handwriting also!

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Will I—what?—give the money myself?—with pleasure! Poor Clara—Why this covers all your savings—and I am so rich!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Nay, I would wish to do all myself!—it is a pride —a duty—it is a joy; and I have so few joys! But, hush!—this way.

div.stage: [They retire into the inner room and converse in dumb show.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: And thus must I grind out my life for ever!—I am ambitious, and Poverty drags me down!—I have learning, and Poverty makes me the drudge of fools!—I love, and Poverty stands like a spectre before the altar! But, no, no—if, as I believe, I am but loved again, I will— will—what?—turn opium-eater, and dream of the Eden I may never enter!

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN
sp.p: Yes, I will get my maid to copy and direct this—she writes well, and her hand will never be discovered. I will have it done and sent instantly.

div.stage: Clara advances to the front of the stage, and seats herself—Evelyn reading—Enter Sir Frederick Blount.

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: No one in the woom!—Oh, Miss Douglas!—Pway don't let me disturb you. Where is Miss Vesey— Georgina?

sp.speaker: Evelyn
sp.stage: (looking up, gives Clara a chair, and re-seats himself).
sp.p: Insolent puppy!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Shall I tell her you are here, Sir Frederick?

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: Not for the world—vewy pwetty girl this companion!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: What did you think of the Panorama the other day, cousin Evelyn?

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: “I cannot talk with civet in the room, A fine puss gentleman that's all perfume!” Rather good lines these.

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: Sir!

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: Don't you think so?—Cowper.

sp.speaker: BLOUNT
sp.p: Cowper!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Cowper.

sp.speaker: BLOUNT
sp.p: Stwange person, Mr. Evelyn!—quite a chawacter!— Indeed the Panowama gives you no idea of Naples— a delightful place. I make it a wule to go there evewy second year—I am vewy fond of twavelling. You'd like Wome (Rome)—bad inns, but vewy fine wuins; gives you quite a taste for that sort of thing!

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: “How much a dunce that has been sent to roam Excels a dunce that has been kept at home.”

sp.speaker: BLOUNT
sp.p: That fellow Cowper says vewy odd things!— Humph!—it is beneath me to quawwell.—

It will not take long to wead the will, I suppose. Poor old Mordaunt—I am his nearest male welation. He was vewy eccentwic. By the way, Miss Douglas, did you wemark my cuwicle? It is bwinging cuwicles into fashion. I should be most happy if you would allow me to dwive you out. Nay—nay—I should, upon my word.

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: A wasp!—a wasp!—just going to settle. Take care of the wasp, Miss Douglas!

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: A wasp!—where?—don't bwing it this way?—some people don't mind them! I've a particular dislike to wasps; they sting damnably!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: I beg pardon—it's only a gad-fly.

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: Sir John will be happy to see you in his study, Sir Frederick.

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: Vewy well. Upon my word, there is something vewy nice about this girl. To be sure, I love Georgina —but if this one would take a fancy to me
—Well, I don't see what harm it could do me! —Au plaisir!

div.head: SCENE IV.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Clara!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Cousin!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: And you too are a dependant!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: But on Lady Franklin, who seeks to make me forget it.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Ay, but can the world forget it? This insolent condescension—this coxcombry of admiration— more galling than the arrogance of contempt!—Look you now—Robe Beauty in silk and cachemire—hand Virtue into her chariot—lackey their caprices—wrap them from the winds—fence them round with a golden circle—and Virtue and Beauty are as goddesses, both to peasant and to prince. Strip them of the adjuncts— see Beauty and Virtue poor—dependent—solitary— walking the world defenceless; oh, then, the devotion changes its character—the same crowd gather eagerly around—fools—fops—libertines—not to worship at the shrine, but to sacrifice the victim!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: My cousin, you are cruel!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Forgive me! There is a something, when a man's heart is better than his fortunes, that makes even affection bitter. Mortification for myself—it has ceased to chafe me. I can mock where I once resented. But you—YOU, so delicately framed and nurtured—one slight to you—one careless look—one disdainful tone— makes me feel the true curse of the poor man. His pride gives armour to his own breast, but it has no shield to protect another!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: But I too have pride of my own—I too can smile at the pointless insolence—

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Smile—and he took your hand!—Oh, Clara, you know not the tortures that I suffer hourly! When others approach you—young—fair—rich—the sleek darlings of the world—I accuse you of your very beauty —I writhe beneath every smile that you bestow. No —speak not!—my heart has broke its silence, and you shall hear the rest. For you I have endured the weary bondage of this house—the fool's gibe—the hireling's sneer—the bread, purchased by toils, that should have led me to loftier ends: yes, to see you—hear you— breathe the same air—be ever at hand—that if others slighted, from one at least you might receive the luxury of respect:—for this—for this I have lingered, suffered, and forborne. Oh, Clara! we are orphans both—friendless both; you are all in the world to me: turn not away—my very soul speaks in these words—I LOVE YOU!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: No—Evelyn—Alfred—No! say it not—think it not! it were madness.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Madness!—Nay, hear me yet. I am poor—penniless —a beggar for bread to a dying servant. True!— But I have a heart of iron! I have knowledge— patience—health,—and my love for you gives me at last ambition! I have trifled with my own energies till now, for I despised all things till I loved thee! With you to toil for—your step to support—your path to smoothe—and I—I, poor Alfred Evelyn—promise at last to win for you even fame and fortune! Do not withdraw your hand—this hand—shall it not be mine?

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Ah, Evelyn! Never—never!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Never!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Forget this folly; our union is impossible, and to talk of love were to deceive both!

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: Because I am poor!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: And I too! A marriage of privation—of penury— of days that dread the morrow! I have seen such a lot! Never return to this again.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Enough—you are obeyed. I deceived myself—ha!— ha!—I fancied that I too was loved. I, whose youth is already half gone with care and toil!—whose mind is soured—whom nobody can love—who ought to have loved no one!

sp.speaker: CLARA
sp.p: And if it were only I to suffer, or perhaps to starve! —Oh, what shall I say? Evelyn—Cousin?

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Madam.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Alfred—I—I—

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Reject me!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Yes! It is past!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Let me think. It was yesterday her hand trembled when mine touched it. And the rose I gave her— yes, she pressed her lips to it once when she seemed as if she saw me not. But it was a trap—a trick—for I was as poor then as now. This will be a jest for them all! Well, courage! it is but a poor heart that a coquet's contempt can break! And now that I care for no one, the world is but a great chess-board, and I will sit down in earnest and play with Fortune!

div.stage: Enter Lord Glossmore preceded by Servant.

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: I will tell Sir John, my Lord!

sp.speaker: GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: The secretary—hum!—Fine day, Sir; any news from the East?

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Yes!—all the wise men have gone back there!

sp.speaker: GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: Ha, ha!—not all, for here comes Mr. Stout, the great political economist.

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: Good morning, Glossmore.

sp.speaker: GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: Glossmore!—the Parvenu!

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: Afraid I might be late—Been detained at the Vestry —Astonishing how ignorant the English poor are!— Took me an hour and a half to beat it into the head of a stupid old widow, with nine children, that to allow her three shillings a-week was against all the rules of public morality!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Excellent!—admirable!—your hand, Sir!

sp.speaker: GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: What! you approve such doctrines, Mr. Evelyn? Are old Women women only fit to be starved!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Starved! popular delusion! Observe, my Lord— to squander money upon those who starve is only to afford encouragement to starvation!

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: A very superior person that!

sp.speaker: GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: Atrocious principles! Give me the good old times when it was the duty of the rich to succour the distressed.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: On second thoughts, you are right, my Lord. I, too, know a poor woman—ill—dying—in want. Shall she, too, perish?

sp.speaker: GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: Perish! horrible!—in a Christian country. Perish! Heaven forbid!

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: What, then, will you give her?

sp.speaker: GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: Ehem! Sir—the parish ought to give.

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: No!—No—No. Certainly not!

sp.speaker: GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: No! no! But I say yes! yes! And if the parish refuse to maintain the poor, the only way left to a man of firmness and resolution, holding the principles that I do, and adhering to the constitution of our fathers, is to force the poor on the parish by never giving them a farthing oneself.

div.head: SCENE VI.
div.stage: Sir John, Blount, Lady Franklin, Georgina, Glossmore, Stout, Evelyn.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: How d'ye do!—Ah! How d'ye do, gentlemen? This is a most melancholy meeting! The poor deceased! —what a man he was!

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: I was chwistened Fwedewick after him! He was my first cousin.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: And Georgina his own niece—next of kin!—an excellent man, though odd—a kind heart, but no liver! I sent him twice a-year thirty dozen of the Cheltenham waters. It's a comfort to reflect on these little attentions at such a time.

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: And I, too, sent him the Parliamentary Debates regularly, bound in calf. He was my second cousin— sensible man—and a follower of Malthus: never married to increase the surplus population, and fritter away his money on his own children. And now—

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: He reaps the benefit of celibacy in the prospective gratitude of every cousin he had in the world!

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Hush! hush! decency, Lady Franklin; decency!

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: Mr. Graves—Mr. Sharp.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Oh, here's Mr. Graves; that's Sharp, the lawyer, who brought the will from Calcutta.

div.head: SCENE VII.

sp.speaker: Chorus of Sir John, Glossmore, Blount, Stout.
sp.p: Ah, Sir—Ah, Mr. Graves!

div.stage: [Georgina holds her handkerchief to her eyes.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: A sad occasion!

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: But everything in life is sad. Be comforted, Miss Vesey. True, you have lost an uncle; but I—I have lost a wife—such a wife!—the first of her sex—and the second cousin of the defunct! Excuse me, Sir John; at the sight of your mourning my wounds bleed afresh.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Take some refreshment—a glass of wine.

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Thank you!—(very fine sherry!)—Ah! my poor sainted Maria! Sherry was her wine: everything reminds me of Maria! Ah, Lady Franklin! you knew her. Nothing in life can charm me now.
A monstrous fine woman that!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: And now to business. Evelyn, you may retire.

sp.speaker: SHARP
sp.p: Evelyn—any relation to Alfred Evelyn?

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: The same.

sp.speaker: SHARP.
sp.p: Cousin to the deceased, seven times removed. Be seated, Sir; there may be some legacy, though trifling: all the relations, however distant, should be present.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Then Clara is related—I will go for her.

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: Ah, Mr. Evelyn; I hope you will come in for something —a few hundreds, or even more.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Silence! Hush! Whugh! ugh! Attention.

div.stage: (While the Lawyer opens the Will, re-enter Lady Franklin and Clara.)

sp.speaker: SHARP.
sp.p: The will is very short—being all personal property. He was a man that always came to the point.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: I wish there were more like him!—

sp.speaker: SHARP
sp.p: “I, Frederick James Mordaunt, of Calcutta, being, at the present date, of sound mind, though infirm body, do hereby give, will, and bequeath—imprimis, to my second cousin, Benjamin Stout, Esq., of Pall-Mall, London—
Being the value of the Parliamentary Debates, with which he has been pleased to trouble me for some time past—deducting the carriage thereof, which he always forgot to pay—the sum of 14l. 2s. 4d.

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: Eh, what!—14l.? Oh, hang the old miser!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Decency—decency! Proceed, Sir.

sp.speaker: SHARP.
sp.p: “Item.—To Sir Frederick Blount, Baronet, my nearest male relative—

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: Poor old boy!

div.stage: [Georgina puts her arm over Blount's chair.

sp.speaker: SHARP.
sp.p: “Being, as I am informed, the best-dressed young gentleman in London, and in testimony to the only merit I ever heard he possessed, the sum of 500l. to buy a dressing-case.

div.stage: [Chorus breathe more freely; Georgina catches her father's eye, and removes her arm.

sp.speaker: BLOUNT
sp.p: Ha! Ha! Ha! Vewy poor wit—low!—vewy—vewy low!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Silence, now, will you?

sp.speaker: SHARP.
sp.p: “Item.—To Charles Lord Glossmore—who asserts that he is my relation—my collection of dried butterflies, and the pedigree of the Mordaunts from the reign of King John.

sp.speaker: GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: Butterflies!—Pedigree!—I disown the plebeian!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN
sp.p: Upon my word, this is too revolting! Decency— go on.

sp.speaker: SHARP.
sp.p: “Item.—To Sir John Vesey, Baronet, Knight of the Guelph, F.R.S., F.S.A., &c.—

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Hush! Now it is really interesting!

sp.speaker: SHARP.
sp.p: “Who married my sister, and who sends me every year the Cheltenham waters, which nearly gave me my death —I bequeath—the empty bottles.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Why, the ungrateful, rascally, old—

sp.speaker: CHORUS.
sp.p: Decency, Sir John—decency!

sp.speaker: SHARP.
sp.p: “Item.—To Henry Graves, Esq., of the Albany—

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Pooh, gentlemen—my usual luck—not even a ring, I dare swear!

sp.speaker: SHARP.
sp.p: “The sum of 5000l. in the Three per Cents.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: I wish you joy!

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Joy—pooh! Three per Cents!—Funds sure to go! Had it been land, now—though only an acre!—just like my luck.

sp.speaker: SHARP.
sp.p: “Item.—To my niece Georgina Vesey—

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Ah, now it comes!

sp.speaker: SHARP.
sp.p: “The sum of 10,000l. India stock, being, with her father's reputed savings, as much as a single woman ought to possess.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: And what the devil, then, does the old fool do with all his money?

sp.speaker: CHORUS.
sp.p: Really, Sir John, this is too revolting. Decency! Hush!

sp.speaker: SHARP.
sp.p: “And, with the aforesaid legacies and exceptions, I do will and bequeath the whole of my fortune, in India stock, Bonds, Exchequer bills, Three per Cents, Consols, and in the Bank of Calcutta (constituting him hereby sole residuary legatee and joint executor with the aforesaid Henry Graves, Esq.), to Alfred Evelyn, now or formerly of Trinity College, Cambridge—

sp.speaker: SHARP.
sp.p: “Being, I am told, an oddity, like myself—the only one of my relations who never fawned on me, and who, having known privation, may the better employ wealth.”—And now, Sir, I have only to wish you joy, and give you this letter from the deceased—I believe it is important.

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: Ah, Clara, if you had but loved me!

sp.speaker: CLARA
sp.p: And his wealth, even more than poverty, separates us for ever!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN
sp.p: Go, child—put a good face on it—he's an immense match! My dear fellow, I wish you joy: you are a great man now—a very great man!

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: And her voice alone is silent!

sp.speaker: LORD GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: If I can be of any use to you—

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: Or I, Sir—

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: Or I? Shall I put you up at the clubs?

sp.speaker: SHARP.
sp.p: You will want a man of business. I transacted all Mr. Mordaunt's affairs.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Tush, tush! Mr. Evelyn is at home here—always looked on him as a son! Nothing in the world we would not do for him! Nothing!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Lend me 10l. for my old nurse!

div.stage: [Chorus put their hands into their pockets.

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: An anteroom in Evelyn's new house; at one corner, behind a large screen, Mr. Sharp writing at a desk, books and parchments before him.—Mr. Crimson, the portrait-painter; Mr. Grab, the publisher; Mr. MacStucco, the architect; Mr. Tabouret, the upholsterer; Mr. Macfinch, the silversmith; Mr. Patent, the coachmaker; Mr. Kite, the horse-dealer; and Mr. Frantz, the tailor.—(Servants in livery cross to and fro the Stage.)

sp.speaker: PATENT
sp.p: Yes, sir; this is the Evelyn vis-à-vis! No one more the fashion than Mr. Evelyn. Money makes the man, sir.

sp.speaker: FRANTZ.
sp.p: But de tailor, de schneider, make de gentleman! It is Mr. Frantz, of St. James's, who take his measure and his cloth, and who make de fine handsome noblemen and gentry, where de faders and de mutters make only de ugly little naked boys!

sp.speaker: MACSTUCCO.
sp.p: He's a mon o' teeste, Mr. Evelyn. He taulks o' buying a veela (villa), just to pool dune and build oop again. Ah, Mr. Macfinch, a design for a piece of pleete, eh!

sp.speaker: MACFINCH
sp.p: Yees, sir, the shield o' Alexander the Great, to hold ices and lemonade! It will coost two thousand poond!

sp.speaker: MACSTUCCO.
sp.p: And it's dirt cheap—ye're Scotch, arn't ye?

sp.speaker: MACFINCH.
sp.p: Aberdounshire!—scraitch me, and I'll scraitch you!

div.stage: Door at the back thrown open.—Enter Evelyn.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: A levee, as usual. Good day. Ah, Tabouret, your designs for the draperies; very well.—And what do you want, Mr. Crimson?

sp.speaker: CRIMSON.
sp.p: Sir, if you'd let me take your portrait, it would make my fortune. Every one says you're the finest judge of paintings.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Of paintings! paintings! Are you sure I'm a judge of paintings?

sp.speaker: CRIMSON.
sp.p: Oh, sir, did'nt you buy the great Correggio for 4000l.?

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: True—I see. So 4000l. makes me an excellent judge of paintings. I'll call on you, Mr. Crimson,— good day. Mr. Grab—oh, you're the publisher who once refused me 5l. for my poem? you are right, it was sad doggrel.

sp.speaker: GRAB.
sp.p: Doggrel! Mr. Evelyn, it was sublime! But times were bad then.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Very bad times with me.

sp.speaker: GRAB.
sp.p: But, now, Sir, if you give me the preference, I'll push it, Sir,—I'll push it! I only publish for poets in high life, Sir; and a gentleman of your station ought to be pushed!—500l. for the poem, Sir!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: 500l. when I don't want it, where 5l. once would have seemed a fortune.“Now I am rich, what value in the lines! How the wit brightens,—how the sense refines!”

div.stage: [Turns to the rest, who surround him.

sp.speaker: KITE.
sp.p: Thirty young horses from Yorkshire, sir!

sp.speaker: PATENT
sp.p: The Evelyn vis-à-vis!

sp.speaker: MACFINCH
sp.p: The Evelyn salver!

sp.speaker: FRANTZ
sp.p: Sare, I have brought de coat—de great Evelyn coat;

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Oh, go to—that is, go home! Make me as celebrated for vis-à-vis', salvers, furniture, and coats, as I already am for painting, and shortly shall be for poetry. I resign myself to you—go!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Stout, you look heated!

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: I hear you have just bought the great Groginhole property.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: It is true. Sharp says it's a bargain.

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: Well, my dear friend Hopkins, member for Groginhole, can't live another month—but the interests of mankind forbid regret for individuals! The patriot Popkins intends to start for the boro' the instant Hopkins is dead!—your interest will secure his election! —now is your time!—put yourself forward in the march of enlightenment!—By all that is bigoted here comes Glossmore!

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Stout, Glossmore, Evelyn; Sharp, still at his desk.

sp.speaker: GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: So lucky to find you at home! Hopkins, of Groginhole, is not long for this world. Popkins, the brewer, is already canvassing underhand (so very ungentleman-like!). Keep your interest for young Lord Cipher—a most valuable candidate. This is an awful moment— the CONSTITUTION depends on his return! Vote for Cipher!

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: Popkins is your man!

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: Cipher and Popkins—Popkins and Cipher! Enlightenment and Popkins—Cipher and the Constitution! I am puzzled! Stout, I am not known at Groginhole.

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: Your property's known there!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: But purity of election—independence of votes—

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: To be sure: Cipher bribes abominably. Frustrate his schemes—preserve the liberties of the borough— turn every man out of his house who votes against enlightenment and Popkins!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Right!—down with those who take the liberty to admire any liberty except our liberty! That is liberty!

sp.speaker: GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: Cipher has a stake in the country—will have 50,000l. a-year—Cipher will never give a vote without considering beforehand how people of 50,000l. a-year will be affected by the motion.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Right: for, as without law there would be no property, so to be the law for property is the only proper property of law!—That is law!

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: Popkins is all for economy—there's a sad waste of the public money—they give the Speaker 5000l. a-year, when I've a brother-in-law who takes the chair at the vestry, and who assures me confidentially he'd consent to be Speaker for half the money!

sp.speaker: GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: Enough, Mr. Stout.—Mr. Evelyn has too much at stake for a leveller.

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: And too much sense for a bigot.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Mr. Evelyn has no politics at all!—Did you ever play at battledore?

sp.speaker: BOTH.
sp.p: Battledore!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Battledore!—that is, a contest between two parties: both parties knock about something with singular skill —something is kept up—high—low—here—there— everywhere—nowhere! How grave are the players! how anxious the bystanders! how noisy the battledores! But when this something falls to the ground, only fancy—it's nothing but cork and feather! Go, and play by yourselves—I'm no hand at it!

sp.speaker: STOUT
sp.p: Sad ignorance!—Aristocrat!

sp.speaker: GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: Heartless principles!—Parvenu!

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: Then you don't go against us?—I'll bring Popkins to-morrow.

sp.speaker: GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: Keep yourself free till I present Cipher to you.

sp.speaker: STOUT.
sp.p: I must go to inquire after Hopkins. The return of Popkins will be an era in history.

sp.speaker: GLOSSMORE.
sp.p: I must be off to the club—the eyes of the country are upon Groginhole. If Cipher fail, the constitution is gone!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Sharp, come here—let me look at you! You are my agent, my lawyer, my man of business. I believe you honest;—but what is honesty?—where does it exist? —in what part of us?

sp.speaker: SHARP.
sp.p: In the heart, I suppose, sir.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Mr. Sharp, it exists in the breeches' pocket! Observe, I lay this piece of yellow earth on the table—I contemplate you both;—the man there—the gold here! Now, there is many a man in those streets honest as you are, who moves, thinks, feels, and reasons as well as we do; excellent in form—imperishable in soul; who, if his pockets were three days empty, would sell thought, reason, body, and soul too, for that little coin! Is that the fault of the man?—no! it is the fault of mankind! God made man; behold what mankind have made a god! When I was poor I hated the world; now I am rich I despise it! Fools— knaves—hypocrites!—By the by, Sharp, send 100l. to the poor bricklayer whose house was burnt down yesterday.
Ah, Graves, my dear friend! what a world this is! —a cur of a world, that fawns on its master, and bites the beggar! Ha! ha! it fawns on me now, for the beggar has bought the cur!

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: It is an atrocious world!—but it will be burnt one day, and that's some comfort!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Every hour brings its gloomy lesson—the temper sours—the affections wither—the heart hardens into stone! Zounds, Sharp! what do you stand gaping there for?—have you no bowels?—why don't you go and see to the bricklayer?

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Graves, of all my new friends—and their name is Legion—you are the only one I esteem; there is sympathy between us—we take the same views of life. I am cordially glad to see you!

sp.speaker: GRAVES
sp.p: Ah! why should you be glad to see a man so miserable?

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Because I am miserable myself!

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: You! Pshaw! you have not been condemned to lose a wife!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: But, plague on it, man, I may be condemned to take one!—Sit down, and listen. I want a confidant!— Left fatherless, when yet a boy, my poor mother grudged herself food, to give me education. Some one had told her that learning was better than house and land—that's a lie, Graves.

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: A scandalous lie, Evelyn!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: On the strength of that lie I was put to school—sent to college, a sizar. Do you know what a sizar is? In pride he is a gentleman—in knowledge he is a scholar —and he crawls about, amidst gentlemen and scholars, with the livery of a pauper on his back! I carried off the great prizes—I became distinguished—I looked to a high degree, leading to a fellowship; that is, an independence for myself—a home for my mother. One day a young lord insulted me—I retorted—he struck me— refused apology—refused redress. I was a sizar!—a Pariah!—a thing to be struck! Sir, I was at least a man, and I horsewhipped him in the hall before the eyes of the whole College! A few days, and the lord's chastisement was forgotten. The next day the sizar was expelled—the career of a life blasted. That is the difference between Rich and Poor: it takes a whirlwind to move the one—a breath may uproot the other! I came to London. As long as my mother lived I had one to toil for; and I did toil—did hope—did struggle to be something yet. She died, and then, somehow, my spirit broke—I resigned myself to my fate; the Alps above me seemed too high to ascend—I ceased to care what became of me. At last I submitted to be the poor relation—the hanger-on and gentleman-lackey of Sir John Vesey. But I had an object in that—there was one in that house whom I had loved at the first sight.

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: And were you loved again?

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: I fancied it, and was deceived. Not an hour before I inherited this mighty wealth, I confessed my love, and was rejected because I was poor. Now, mark: you remember the letter which Sharp gave me when the will was read?

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Perfectly: what were the contents?

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: After hints, cautions, and admonitions—half in irony, half in earnest (Ah, poor Mordaunt had known the world!), it proceeded—but I'll read it to you:—“Having selected you as my heir, because I think money a trust to be placed where it seems likely to be best employed, I now—not impose a condition, but ask a favour. If you have formed no other and insuparable attachment, I could wish to suggest your choice: my two nearest female relations are my niece Georgina, and my third cousin, Clara Douglas, the daughter of a once dear friend. If you could see in either of these one whom you could make your wife, such would be a marriage that, if I live long enough to return to England, I would seek to bring about before I die.” My friend, this is not a legal condition—the fortune does not rest on it; yet, need I say that my gratitude considers it a moral obligation? Several months have elapsed since thus called upon—I ought now to decide: you hear the names— Clara Douglas is the woman who rejected me!

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: But now she would accept you!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: And do you think I am so base a slave to passion, that I would owe to my gold what was denied to my affection?

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: But you must choose one, in common gratitude; you ought to do so—yes, there you are right. Besides, you are constantly at the house—the world observes it: you must have raised hopes in one of the girls. Yes; it is time to decide between her whom you love, and her whom you do not!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Of the two, then, I would rather marry where I should exact the least. A marriage, to which each can bring sober esteem and calm regard, may not be happiness, but it may be content. But to marry one whom you could adore, and whose heart is closed to you—to yearn for the treasure, and only to claim the casket— to worship the statue that you never may warm to life —Oh! such a marriage would be a hell the more terrible because Paradise was in sight.

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Georgina is pretty, but vain and frivolous.—
But he has no right to be fastidious—he has never known Maria!—
Yes, my dear friend, now I think on it, you will be as wretched as myself!—When you are married we will mingle our groans together!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: You may misjudge Georgina; she may have a nobler nature than appears on the surface. On the day, but before the hour, in which the will was read, a letter, in a strange or disguised hand, signed “From an unknown friend to Alfred Evelyn,” and enclosing what to a girl would have been a considerable sum, was sent to a poor woman for whom I had implored charity, and whose address I had given only to Georgina.

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Why not assure yourself?

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Because I have not dared. For sometimes, against my reason, I have hoped that it might be Clara!
sp.stage: (taking a letter from his bosom and looking at it).
sp.p: No, I can't recognise the hand. Graves, I detest that girl!

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Who? Georgina?

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: No; Clara! But I've already, thank Heaven! taken some revenge upon her. Come nearer.
I've bribed Sharp to say that Mordaunt's letter to me contained a codicil leaving Clara Douglas 20,000l.

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: And didn't it? How odd, then, not to have mentioned her in his will.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: One of his caprices: besides, Sir John wrote him word that Lady Franklin had adopted her. But I'm glad of it—I've paid the money—she's no more a dependant. No one can insult her now—she owes it all to me, and does not guess it, man—does not guess it! —owes it to me, me whom she rejected;—me, the poor scholar!—Ha! ha!—there's some spite in that, Eh?

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: You're a fine fellow, Evelyn, and we understand each other. Perhaps Clara may have seen the address, and dictated this letter, after all!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Do you think so?—I'll go to the house this instant!

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Eh? Humph! Then I'll go with you. That Lady Franklin is a fine woman! If she were not so gay, I think—I could—

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: No; no; don't think any such thing: women are even worse than men.

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: True; to love is a boy's madness!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: To feel is to suffer!

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: To hope is to be deceived.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: I have done with romance!

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Mine is buried with Maria!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: If Clara did but write this!—

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Make haste, or Lady Franklin will be out!—A vale of tears—a vale of tears!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: A vale of tears, indeed!
And I left my hat behind me! Just like my luck! If I had been bred a hatter, little boys would have come into the world without heads.

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: Drawing-rooms at Sir John Vesey's, as in Scene I., Act I.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Past two, and I have so many places to go to. Tell Philipps I want the carriage directly—instantly.

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: I beg pardon, my Lady; Philipps told me to say the young horse had fallen lame, and could not be used today.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Well, on second thought, that is lucky; now I have an excuse for not making a great many tedious visits. I must borrow Sir John's horses for the ball to-night. Oh, Clara, you must see my new turban from Carson's —the prettiest thing in the world, and so becoming!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Ah, Lady Franklin, you'll be so sorry—but—but—

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: But what?

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Such a misfortune! poor Smith is in tears—I promised to break it to you. Your little Charley had been writing his copy, and spilt the ink on the table; and Smith not seeing it—and taking out the turban to put in the pearls as you desired—she—she—

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
CLARA.
sp.p: Dear Lady Franklin, you really have the sweetest temper!

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: I hope so—for it's the most becoming turban a woman can wear! Think of that when you marry. Oh, talking of marriage, I've certainly made a conquest of Mr. Graves.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Mr. Graves! I thought he was inconsolable.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: For his sainted Maria! Poor man! not contented with plaguing him while she lived, she must needs haunt him now she is dead.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: But why does he regret her?

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Why? Because he has everything to make him happy. Easy fortune, good health, respectable character. And since it is his delight to be miserable, he takes the only excuse the world will allow him. For the rest—it's the way with widowers; that is, whenever they mean to marry again. But, my dear Clara, you seem absent—pale—unhappy—tears too?

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: No—no—not tears. No!

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Ever since Mr. Mordaunt left you 20,000l. every one admires you. Sir Frederick is desperately smitten.

sp.speaker: CLARA
sp.p: Sir Frederick!

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Ah! Clara, be comforted—I know your secret: I am certain that Evelyn loves you.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: He did—it is past now. He misconceived me when he was poor; and now he is rich, it is not for me to explain.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: My dear child, happiness is too rare to be sacrificed to a scruple. Why does he come here so often?

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Perhaps for Georgina!

div.stage: Enter Sir John, and turns over the books, &c., on the table, as if to look for the newspaper.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Pooh! Georgina is my niece; she is handsome and accomplished—but her father's worldliness has spoilt her nature—she is not worthy of Evelyn! Behind the humour of his irony there is something noble— something that may yet be great. For his sake as well as yours, let me at least—

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Recommend me to his pity! Ah, Lady Franklin! if he addressed me from dictation, I should again refuse him. No; if he cannot read my heart—if he will not seek to read it, let it break unknown.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: You mistake me, my dear child: let me only tell him that you dictated that letter—that you sent that money to his old nurse. Poor Clara! it was your little all. He will then know, at least, if avarice be your sin.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: He would have guessed it, had his love been like mine.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Guessed it—nonsense! The handwriting unknown to him—every reason to think it came from Georgina.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN
sp.p: Hum! Came from Georgina!

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Come, let me tell him this. I know the effect it would have upon his choice.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Choice! oh, that humiliating word! No, Lady Franklin, no! Promise me!

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: But—

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: No! Promise—faithfully—sacredly.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Well, I promise.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: You know how fearful is my character—no infant is more timid: if a poor spider cross the floor, you often laugh to see me grow pale and tremble; and yet I would lay this hand upon the block—I would walk barefoot over the ploughshare of the old ordeal—to save Alfred Evelyn one moment's pain. But I have refused to share his poverty, and I should die with shame if he thought I had now grown enamoured of his wealth. My kind friend, you will keep your promise?

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Yes, since it must be so.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Thanks. I—I—forgive me—I am not well.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: What fools these girls are!—they take as much pains to lose a husband as a poor widow does to get one!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Have you seen the Times newspaper? Where the deuce is the newspaper? I can't find the Times newspaper.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: I think it is in my room. Shall I fetch it?

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: My dear sister—you're the best creature. Do!
Ugh! you unnatural conspirator against your own family! What can this letter be? Ah! I recollect something.

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: Papa, I want—

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Yes, I know what you want well enough! Tell me— were you aware that Clara had sent money to that old nurse Evelyn bored us about the day of the will?

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: No! He gave me the address, and I promised, if—

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Gave you the address?—that's lucky! Hush!

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: Mr. Graves—Mr. Evelyn.

div.head: SCENE V.
div.stage: Graves, Evelyn, Sir John, Georgina, Lady Franklin.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN
sp.p: Here is the newspaper.

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Ay—read the newspapers!—they'll tell you what this world is made of. Daily calendars of roguery and woe! Here, advertisements from quacks, money-lenders, cheap warehouses, and spotted boys with two heads. So much for dupes and imposters! Turn to the other column—police reports, bankruptcies, swindling, forgery, and a biographical sketch of the snubnosed man who murdered his own three little cherubs at Pentonville. Do you fancy these but exceptions to the general virtue and health of the nation?—turn to the leading article! and your hair will stand on end at the horrible wickedness or melancholy idiotism of that half the population who think differently from yourself. In my day I have seen already eighteen crisises, six annihilations of Agriculture and Commerce, four overthrows of the Church, and three last, final, awful, and irremediable destructions of the entire Constitution! And that's a newspaper!

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Ha! ha! your usual vein! always so amusing and good humoured!

sp.speaker: GRAVES
sp.p: Ma'am—good humoured!—

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Ah! you should always wear that agreeable smile; you look so much younger—so much handsomer— when you smile!

sp.speaker: GRAVES
sp.p: Ma'am—A charming creature, upon my word!

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: You have not seen the last H. B.? it is excellent. I think it might make you laugh. But, by-the-by, I don't think you can laugh.

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Ma'am—I have not laughed since the death of my sainted Ma—.

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Ah! and that spiteful Sir Frederick says you never laugh, because—But you'll be angry?

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Angry!—pooh! I despise Sir Frederick too much to let anything he says have the smallest influence over me! He says I don't laugh, because—

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: You have lost your front teeth!

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Lost my front teeth! Upon my word! Ha! ha! ha! That's too good—capital! Ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: LADY FRANKLIN.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha!

div.stage: [They retire to the table in the inner drawing-room.

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: Of course Clara will not appear!—avoids me as usual! But what do I care?—what is she to me? Nothing! I'll swear this is her glove!—no one else has so small a hand. She'll miss it—so—so! Nobody's looking—I'll keep it, just to vex her.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN
sp.p: Yes—yes—leave me to manage: you took his portrait, as I told you.

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: Yes—but I could not catch the expression. I got Clara to touch it up.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: That girl's always in the way!

sp.speaker: SMOOTH.
sp.p: Good morning, dear John. Ah, Miss Vesey, you have no idea of the conquests you made at Almack's last night!

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.stage: (examining him curiously while Smooth is talking to Georgina).
sp.p: And that's the celebrated Dudley Smooth!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: More commonly called Deadly Smooth!—the finest player at whist, écarté, billiards, chess, and piquet, between this and the Pyramids—the sweetest manners! —always calls you by your Christian name. But take care how you play at cards with him!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: He does not cheat, I suppose?

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Hist! No!—but he always wins! Eats up a brace of lords and a score or two of guardsmen every season, and runs through a man's fortune like a course of the Carlsbad waters. He's an uncommonly clever fellow!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Clever? yes! When a man steals a loaf we cry down the knavery—when a man diverts his neighbour's mill-stream to grind his own corn, we cry up the cleverness!—And every one courts Captain Dudley Smooth!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Why, who could offend him? the best-bred, civilest creature—and a dead shot! There is not a cleverer man in the three kingdoms.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: A study—a study!—let me examine him! Such men are living satires on the world.

sp.speaker: SMOOTH
sp.stage: (passing his arm caressingly over Sir John's shoulder).
sp.p: My dear John, how well you are looking! A new lease of life! Introduce me to Mr. Evelyn.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Sir, it's an honour I've long ardently desired.

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: How d'ye do, Sir John. Ah, Evelyn—I wished so much to see you!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: 'Tis my misfortune to be visible!

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: A little this way. You know, perhaps, that I once paid my addwesses to Miss Vesey; but since that vewy eccentwic will Sir John has shuffled me off, and hints at a pwior attachment—
which I know to be false.

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: A prior attachment!—(Ha! Clara!) Well, another time, my dear Blount.

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: Stay a moment—I want you to do me a favour with regard to Miss Douglas!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Miss Douglas!

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: Yes;—you see, though Georgina has great expectations, and Stingy Jack will leave her all that he has, yet she has only her legacy of 10,000l. at the moment— no doubt closely settled on herself too: Clawa has 20,000l. And, I think, Clawa always liked me a little.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: You! I dare say she did!

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: It is whispered about that you mean to pwopose to Georgina. Nay, Sir John more than hinted that was her pwior attachment!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Indeed!

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: Now, as you are all in all with the family, if you could say a word for me to Miss Douglas, I don't see what harm it could do me!—
I will punish Georgina for her puerfidy.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: 'Sdeath, man! speak for yourself! you are just the sort of man for young ladies to like—they understand you—you're of their own level. Pshaw! you're too modest—you want no mediator!

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: My dear fellow, you flatter me. I'm well enough in my way. But you, you know, would cawwy evewything before you!—you're so confoundedly wich!

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: Miss Douglas, what do you think of Sir Frederick Blount? Observe him. He is well dressed—young— tolerably handsome

—bows with an air—has plenty of small talk—everything to captivate. Yet he thinks that if he and I were suitors to the same lady, I should be more successful because I am richer? What say you? Is love an auction? and do women's hearts go to the highest bidder?

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Their hearts?—No!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: But their hands—yes! You turn away. Ah, you dare not answer that question!

sp.speaker: GEORGINA
sp.p: Sir Frederick flirting with Clara? I'll punish him for his perfidy. You are the last person to talk so, Mr. Evelyn!—you, whose wealth is your smallest attraction —you, whom every one admires, so witty, such taste, such talent! Ah, I'm very foolish!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN
sp.p: You must not turn my little girl's head. Oh, you're a sad fellow! Apropos, I must show you Georgina's last drawings. She has wonderfully improved since you gave her lessons in perspective.

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: No papa—No! pray, no! Nay, don't!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Nonsense, child!—it's very odd, but she's more afraid of you than of any one!

sp.speaker: SMOOTH
sp.p: He's an excellent father, our dear John! and supplies the place of a mother to her.

div.stage: [Turns away to Lady Franklin and Graves.
[Evelyn and Georgina seat themselves, and look over the drawings; Sir John leans over them; Sir Frederick converses with Clara; Evelyn watching them.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Beautiful!—a view from Tivoli. (Death!—she looks down while he speaks to her!) Is there a little fault in that colouring? (She positively blushes!) But this Jupiter is superb. (What a d---d coxcomb it is!)
Oh, she certainly loves him—I too can be loved elsewhere—I too can see smiles and blushes on the face of another!

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: Are you not well?

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: I beg pardon. Yes, you are indeed improved! Ah, who so accomplished as Miss Vesey?

div.stage: [Takes up the drawings; pays her marked attention in dumb show.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Yes, Sir Frederick, the concert was very crowded! Ah, I see that Georgina consoles him for the past! He has only praises for her, nothing but taunts for me!

sp.speaker: BLOUNT.
sp.p: I wish you would take my opewa-box next Saturday —'tis the best in the house. I'm not wich, but I spend what I have on myself! I make a point to have evewything the best in a quiet way. Best opewa-box—best dogs—best horses—best house of its kind. I want nothing to complete my establishment but the best wife!

sp.speaker: CLARA
sp.p: That will come in good time, Sir Frederick.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Oh, it will come—will it? Georgina refused the trifler—she courts him
. Why, what is this?—my own—

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: You must not look at that—you must not indeed. I did not know it was there!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Your own portrait, Evelyn. Why, child! I was not aware you took likenesses?—that's something new! Upon my word it's a strong resemblance.

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: Oh, no—it does not do him justice. Give it to me. I will tear it.—
That odious Sir Frederick!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Nay, you shall not.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: So—so—he loves her then! Misery—misery! But he shall not perceive it! No—no—I can be proud too. Ha! ha!—Sir Frederick—excellent—excellent —you are so entertaining—ha! ha!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Oh, the affectation of coquets—they cannot even laugh naturally!
sp.stage: [Clara looks at him reproachfully, and walks aside with Sir Frederick.
sp.p: But where is the new guitar you meant to buy, Miss Vesey—the one inlaid with tortoiseshell? It is near a year since you set your heart on it, and I don't see it yet!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN
sp.p: The guitar—oh, to tell you a secret—she applied the money I gave her for it to a case of charity several months ago—the very day the will was read. I saw the letter lying on the table, with the money in it. Mind, not a word to her—she'd never forgive me!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Letter!—money! What was the name of the person she relieved?—not Stanton?

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: I don't remember indeed.

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: This is not her hand!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: No! I observed at the time it was not her hand, but I got out from her that she did not wish the thing to be known, and had employed some one else to copy it. May I see the letter? Yes, I think this is the wording. But I did not mean to tell you what case of charity it was. I promised Georgy I would not. Still, how did she know Mrs. Stanton's address?—you never gave it to me!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: I gave it to her, Sir John.

sp.speaker: CLARA
sp.p: Yes, I'll go to the opera, if Lady Franklin will. Do go, dear Lady Franklin!—on Saturday, then, Sir Frederick.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Sir John, to a man like me, this simple act of unostentatious generosity is worth all the accomplishments in the world. A good heart—a tender disposition —a charity that shuns the day—a modesty that blushes at its own excellence—an impulse towards something more divine than Mammon;—such are the true accomplishments which preserve beauty for ever young. Such I have sought in the partner I would take for life;—such I have found—alas! not where I had dreamed!—Miss Vesey, I will be honest—I say, then, frankly—
sp.stage: (as Clara approaches, raising his voice and looking fixedly at her)
sp.p: —I have loved another —deeply—truly—bitterly—vainly!I cannot offer to you, as I did to her, the fair first love of the human heart—rich with all its blossoms and its verdure. But if esteem—if gratitude—if an earnest resolve to conquer every recollection that would wander from your image;—if these can tempt you to accept my hand and fortune, my life shall be a study to deserve your confidence.

div.stage: [Clara stands motionless, clasping her hands, and then slowly seats herself.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: The happiest day of my life!

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: She is pale; she faints! What have I done? Oh, heaven!—Clara!

sp.speaker: CLARA
sp.p: Be happy, my cousin—be happy! Yes, with my whole heart I say it—be happy, Alfred Evelyn!

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: The drawing-rooms in Sir John Vesey's house.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: And he has not pressed you to fix the wedding-day?

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: No; and since he proposed he comes here so seldom, and seems so gloomy. Heigho! Poor Sir Frederick was twenty times more amusing.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: But Evelyn is fifty times as rich!

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: Sir Frederick dresses so well!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: You'll have magnificent diamonds! But a word with you: I saw you yesterday in the square with Sir Frederick; that must not happen again. When a young lady is engaged to one man, nothing is so indecorous as to flirt with another. It might endanger your marriage itself. Oh, it's highly indecorous!

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: Don't be afraid, papa—he takes up with Clara.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Who? Evelyn?

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: Sir Frederick. Heigho!—I hate artful girls.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: The settlements will be splendid! if anything happens, nothing can be handsomer than your jointure.

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: My own kind papa, you always put things so pleasantly. But do you not fear lest he discover that Clara wrote the letter?

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: No; and I shall get Clara out of the house. But there is something else that makes me very uneasy. You know that no sooner did Evelyn come into possession of his fortune than he launched out in the style of a prince. His house in London is a palace, and he has bought a great estate in the country. Look how he lives!—Balls—banquets—fine arts—fiddlers—charities —and the devil to pay!

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: But if he can afford it—

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Oh! as long as he stopped there I had no apprehension; but since he proposed for you he is more extravagant than ever. They say he has taken to gambling! and he is always with Captain Smooth. No fortune can stand Deadly Smooth! If he gets into a scrape he may fall off from the settlements. We must press the marriage at once.

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: Heigho! Poor Frederick! You don't think he is really attached to Clara?

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Upon my word I can't say. Put on your bonnet, and come to Storr and Mortimer's to choose the jewels.

sp.speaker: GEORGINA.
sp.p: The jewels!—yes—the drive will do me good. So you'll send away Clara?—she's so very deceitful.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Never fear—yes—tell her to come to me.

Yes; I must press on this marriage; Georgina has not wit enough to manage him—at least till he's her husband, and then all women find it smooth sailing. This match will make me a man of prodigious importance! I suspect he'll give me up her ten thousand pounds. I can't think of his taking to gambling, for I love him as a son—and I look on his money as my own.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Clara, my love!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Sir—

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: My dear, what I am going to say may appear a little rude and unkind, but you know my character is frankness. —To the point, then: my poor child, I'm aware of your attachment to Mr. Evelyn—

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Sir! my attachment?

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: It is generally remarked. Lady Kind says you are falling away. My poor girl, I pity you—I do, indeed! “Now, there's that letter you wrote to his old nurse—it has got about somehow—and the world is so ill natured. I don't know if I did right; but, after he had proposed to Georgy—(of course not before!) —I thought it so unpleasant for you, as a young lady, to be suspected of anything forward with respect to a man who was not attached to you, that I rather let it be supposed that Georgy herself wrote the letter.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: “Sir, I don't know what right you had to—

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: “That's very true, my dear; and I've been thinking since that I ought perhaps to tell Mr. Evelyn that the letter was yours—shall I?

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: “No, Sir; I beg you will not. I—I”—

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: My dear Clara, don't take on; I would not have said this for the world, if I was not a little anxious about my own girl. Georgina is so unhappy at what every one says of your attachment—

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Every one?—Oh, torture!

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: That it preys on her spirits—it even irritates her temper! You see, though the marriage will take place almost immediately, Mr. Evelyn does not come so often as he ought. In a word, I fear these little jealousies and suspicions will tend to embitter their future union—I'm a father—forgive me.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Embitter their union! Oh, never! What would you have me do, Sir?

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Why, you're now independent. Lady Franklin seems resolved to stay in town. Surely she can't mean to take her money out of the family by some foolish inclination for Mr. Graves! He's always purring and whining about the house, like a black cat in the megrims. What think you, eh?

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Sir, it was of myself—my unhappy self—you were speaking.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: Sly!—True; true! What I meant to say was this:—Lady Franklin persists in staying here: you are your own mistress. Mrs. Carlton, aunt to my late wife, is going abroad for a short time, and would be delighted if you would accompany her.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: It is the very favour I would have asked of you.
I shall escape at least the struggle and the shame. When does she go?

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: In five days—next Monday.—You forgive me?

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: Sir, I thank you.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN
sp.p: Suppose, then, you write a line to her yourself, and settle it at once?

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: The carriage, Sir John; Miss Vesey is quite ready.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: “Wait a moment. Shall I tell Evelyn you wrote the letter?

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: “No, Sir, I implore you.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: “But it would be awkward for Georgy, if discovered.

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: “It never shall be.

sp.speaker: SIR JOHN.
sp.p: “Well, well, as you please. I know nothing could be so painful to a young lady of pride and delicacy.”— James, if Mr. Serious, the clergyman, calls, say I am gone to the great meeting at Exeter Hall: if Lord Spruce calls, say you believe I'm gone to the rehearsal of Cinderella. Oh! and if MacFinch should come— (MacFinch, who duns me three times a-week)—say I've hurried off to Garraways to bid for the great Bulstrode estate. Just put the Duke of Lofty's card carelessly on the hall table. And, I say, James, I expect two gentlemen a little before dinner—Mr. Squab the Radical, and Mr. Qualm of the great Marylebone Conservative Association. Show Squab into the study, and be sure to give him the “Weekly True Sun,”—Qualm into the back parlour with the “Times” and the “Morning Post.” One must have a little management in this world. All humbug!—all humbug, upon my soul!

sp.speaker: CLARA
sp.p: There—it is decided! A few days, and we are parted for ever!—a few weeks, and another will bear his name—his wife! Oh, happy fate! She will have the right to say to him—though the whole world should hear her—“I am thine!” And I embitter their lot—I am the cloud upon their joyous sunshine! And yet, O Alfred! if she loves thee—if she knows thee—if she values thee—and, when thou wrong'st her, if she can forgive, as I do,—I can bless her, when far away, and join her name in my prayers for thee!

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: Miss Vesey just gone? Well, I will write a line.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: So—Clara! Do not let me disturb you, Miss Douglas.

sp.speaker: CLARA
sp.p: Nay, I have done.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: I see that my presence is always odious to you. It is a reason why I come so seldom. But be cheered, Madam: I am here but to fix the day of my marriage, and I shall then go into the country—till—till—In short, this is the last time my visit will banish you from the room I enter.

sp.speaker: CLARA
sp.p: The last time!—and we shall then meet no more!— And to part thus for ever—in scorn—in anger—I cannot bear it!—
Alfred, my cousin, it is true this may be the last time we shall meet—I have made my arrangements to quit England.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: To quit England?

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: But, before I go, let me thank you for many a past kindness, which it is not for an orphan easily to forget.

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: To quit England!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: I have long wished it: but enough of me.—Evelyn, now that you are betrothed to another—now, without recurring to the past—now, without the fear of mutual error and mistake—something of our old friendship may at least return to us.—And if, too, I dared, I have that on my mind which only a friend—a sister— might presume to say to you.

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: Miss Douglas—Clara—if there is aught that I could do—if, while hundreds—strangers—beggars—tell me that I have the power, by opening or shutting this worthless hand, to bid sorrow rejoice or poverty despair —if—if my life—my heart's blood—could render to you one such service as my gold can give to others— why, speak!—and the past you allude to,—yes, even that bitter past,—I will cancel and forget!

sp.speaker: CLARA
sp.p: We are friends, then!—you are again my cousin!— my brother!

sp.speaker: EVELYN
sp.p: Brother!—Ah! say on!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: I speak, then, as a sister—herself weak, inexperienced, ignorant, nothing—might speak to a brother, in whose career she felt the ambition of a man. Oh, Evelyn! when you inherited this vast wealth I pleased myself with imagining how you would wield the power delegated to your hands. I knew your benevolence— your intellect—your genius!—the ardent mind couched beneath the cold sarcasm of a long-baffled spirit! I saw before me the noble and bright career open to you at last—and I often thought that, in after years, when far away—as I soon shall be—I should hear your name identified, not with what fortune can give the base, but with deeds and ends to which, for the great, fortune is but the instrument;—I often thought that I should say to my own heart—weeping proud and delicious tears— “And once this man loved me!”

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: No more, Clara!—oh, heavens!—no more!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: But has it been so?—have you been true to your own self?—Pomp—parade—luxuries—pleasures—follies! —all these might distinguish others, they do but belie the ambition and the soul of Alfred Evelyn!—Oh! pardon me—I am too bold—I pain—I offend you.— Ah, I should not have dared thus much had I not thought, at times, that—that—

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: That these follies—these vanities—this dalliance with a loftier fate—were your own work! You thought that, and you were right! Perhaps, indeed, after a youth steeped to the lips in the hyssop and gall of penury—perhaps I might have wished royally to know the full value of that dazzling and starry life which, from the last step in the ladder, I had seen indignantly and from afar. But a month—a week—would have sufficed for that experience. Experience!—Oh, how soon we learn that hearts are as cold and souls as vile—no matter whether the sun shine on the noble in his palace, or the rain drench the rags of the beggar cowering at the porch. The extremes of life differ but in this:— Above, Vice smiles and revels—below, Crime frowns and starves. But you—did not you reject me because I was poor? Despise me if you please!—my revenge might be unworthy—I wished to show you the luxuries, the gaud, the splendour I thought you prized,—to surround with the attributes your sex seems most to value the station that, had you loved me, it would have been yours to command. But vain—vain alike my poverty and my wealth! You loved me not in either, and my fate is sealed!

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: A happy fate, Evelyn!—you love!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: And at last I am beloved.—
sp.stage: (After a pause, and turning to her abruptly)
sp.p: Do you doubt it?

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: No, I believe it firmly!—
Were it possible for her not to love him?

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Georgina, perhaps, is vain—and light—and—

sp.speaker: CLARA.
sp.p: No—think it not! Once removed from the worldly atmosphere of her father's councils, and you will form and raise her to your own level. She is so young yet— she has beauty, cheerfulness, and temper;—the rest you will give, if you will but yet do justice to your own nature. And, now that there is nothing unkind between us—not even regret—and surely
not revenge, my cousin—you will rise to your nobler self— and so, farewell!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: No; stay—one moment;—you still feel interest in my fate! Have I been deceived? Oh, why—why did you spurn the heart whose offerings were lavished at your feet? Could you still—still—? Distraction —I know not what I say!—my honour pledged to another—my vows accepted and returned! Go, Clara; it is best so! Yet you will miss some one, perhaps, more than me—some one to whose follies you have been more indulgent—some one to whom you would permit a yet tenderer name than that of brother!

sp.speaker: CLARA
sp.p: It will make him, perhaps, happier to think it!— Think so, if you will!—but part friends.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Friends—and that is all! Look you, this is life!— The eyes that charmed away every sorrow—the hand whose lightest touch thrilled to the very core—the presence that, like moonlight, shed its own hallowing beauty over the meanest things;—a little while—a year—a month—a day—and we smile that we could dream so idly. All—all—the sweet enchantment, known but once, never to return again, vanished from the world! And the one who forgets the soonest—the one who robs your earth for ever of its summer—comes to you with a careless lip, and says—“Let us part friends!” —Go, Clara,—go,—and be happy if you can!

sp.speaker: CLARA
sp.p: Cruel—cruel—to the last!—Heaven forgive you, Alfred!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Soft!—let me recall her words, her tones, her looks. Does she love me? She defends her rival—she did not deny it when I charged her with attachment to another: and yet—and yet—there is a voice at my heart which tells me I have been the rash slave of a jealous anger.—But I have made my choice—I must abide the issue!
Lady Franklin is dressing, Sir.

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Well, I'll wait.
She was worthy to have known the lost Maria! So considerate to ask me hither—not to console me, that is impossible—but to indulge the luxury of woe. It will be a mournful scene.—
Is that you, Evelyn?—I have just heard that the borough of Groginhole is vacant at last. Why not stand yourself?—with your property you might come in without even a personal canvass.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: I, who despise these contests for the colour of a straw—this everlasting litigation of Authority versus Man—I to be one of the wranglers?—never!

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: You are quite right, and I beg your pardon.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: And yet Clara spoke of ambition. She would regret me if I could be distinguished.—
To be sure, after all, Graves, corrupt as mankind are, it is our duty to try at least to make them a little better. An Englishman owes something to his country.

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: He does, indeed!
East winds, Fogs, Rheumatism, Pulmonary complaints, and Taxes—
You seem agitated—a quarrel with your intended? Oh! when you've been married a month, you won't know what to do without one!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: You are a pleasant comforter.

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Do you deserve a comforter? One morning you tell me you love Clara, or at least detest her, which is the same thing—(poor Maria often said she detested me)— and that very afternoon you propose to Georgina!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Clara will easily console herself—thanks to Sir Frederick!

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: He is young!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Good looking!

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: A coxcomb!

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: And therefore irresistible!

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: Nevertheless, Clara has had the bad taste to refuse him. I have it from Lady Franklin, to whom he confided his despair in re-arranging his neckcloth.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: My dear friend—is it possible?

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: But what then? You must marry Georgina, who, to believe Lady Franklin, is sincerely attached to— your fortune. Go and hang yourself, Evelyn; you have been duped by them.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: By them—bah! If deceived, I have been my own dupe. Is it not a strange thing that in matters of reason—of the arithmetic and logic of life—we are sensible, shrewd, prudent men? But touch our hearts —move our passions—take us for an instant from the hard safety of worldly calculation—and the philosopher is duller than the fool! Duped—if I thought it!—

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
sp.p: To be sure!—you tried Clara in your poverty; it was a safe experiment to try Georgina in your wealth.

sp.speaker: EVELYN.
sp.p: Ha! that is true—very true. Go on.

sp.speaker: GRAVES.
